y-m-45-01.title: Can we always say 'if perpendicular, the product of the slopes is −1'?
y-m-45-01.topic: The relation between slopes when two lines are perpendicular, and lines that have no slope
y-m-45-01.goal: Using a table of perpendicular line pairs as evidence, judge in what range the statement 'if perpendicular, the product of the slopes is −1' holds, and make lines that satisfy a condition yourself.
y-m-45-01.material:
민재 said, "If two lines are perpendicular to each other, the product of their two slopes is always −1." Below are four pairs of lines on a coordinate plane. (x=2 is read 'x equals 2' and is a vertical line parallel to the y-axis, and y=5 is a horizontal line parallel to the x-axis. y=−x/2+4 is read 'y equals minus x over 2 plus 4', and 3x+2y=6 is read '3x plus 2y equals 6'.)
(가) y=2x+1 and y=−x/2+4
(나) y=3x and y=−3x
(다) x=2 and y=5
(라) 3x+2y=6 and 2x−3y=1
y-m-45-01.thinking.0: Judging a generalization from the evidence in a table
y-m-45-01.thinking.1: Finding the case where the slope is not defined and stating the condition for it to hold
y-m-45-01.thinking.2: Making lines that fit a condition
y-m-45-01.prereq.0: The H2 of this task is only a difficulty level for production assignment and is not a grade assignment in the curriculum. Assume the learner has already studied middle-school linear functions (slope) and the Pythagorean theorem, and equations of lines in high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-45-01.prereq.1: Converting between the forms y=mx+n and ax+by+c=0 of the equation of a line
y-m-45-01.prereq.2: The meaning of slope (understanding the slope of horizontal and vertical lines)
y-m-45-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the pairs that are perpendicular to each other.
y-m-45-01.s.s1.hint.0: In each pair, first read or find the slopes of the two lines and compare the product.
y-m-45-01.s.s1.hint.1: For a pair where it is hard to state the slope, draw how the lines are placed and look at it.
y-m-45-01.s.s1.r.a: This uses the method of reading the two slopes and checking the product.
y-m-45-01.s.s1.o.b: (나) y=3x and y=−3x (passes through the origin)
y-m-45-01.s.s1.r.b: You may have thought that opposite signs of the slope are enough for perpendicular. Multiply the two slopes directly.
y-m-45-01.s.s1.r.c: A vertical line and a horizontal line are hard to describe by slope, so they are easy to miss. Picture the angle the two lines make in a drawing.
y-m-45-01.s.s1.r.d: For the general form, you have to find the slope first before you can look at the product. Rearrange for y and check the slope.
y-m-45-01.s.s1.explain: In (가), the slopes 2 and −1/2 have product −1, and in (라), the slopes −3/2 and 2/3 also have product −1, so they are perpendicular. (다) is a vertical and a horizontal line, so it is perpendicular. In (나), the slopes are 3 and −3, so the product is −9 and they are not perpendicular.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.prompt: Using (가) to (라) as evidence, judge 민재's statement.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.hint.0: First check whether you can find the product of the slopes for each perpendicular pair in the table.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.hint.1: If there is a perpendicular pair for which you cannot find the product, compare how that pair changes the statement.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.o.a: False. (다) is perpendicular but the product of the slopes cannot be found, so the statement should be seen as not right as it stands.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.r.a: You took (다) as a counterexample and judged it false. Judging by one counterexample is a good method. Go on to think about the range in which it is true.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.o.b: True. In the perpendicular pairs (가) and (라) the product is −1, so I think it can be seen to hold always.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.r.b: Two right examples do not make it 'always'. Look at whether there is a pair in the table that does not fit.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.o.c: It is right only for lines that have slopes. Pairs that include a vertical line must be looked at separately.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.r.c: If you narrow the range to the case where slopes exist, this statement is right. This is a judgment that states the range.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.o.d: Cannot judge. Until we investigate more lines, we cannot know whether it is true or false.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.r.d: A statement of 'always' can be judged by one example that does not fit. Look for whether there is such an example in the table.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.explain: For two lines whose slopes are defined (neither is a vertical line), if they are perpendicular the product is −1. When a vertical line is included, as in (다), the slope is not defined, so you cannot talk about the product. So writing that it is false, or stating the range as 'only when the slopes exist', are both reasonable.
y-m-45-01.s.s2.acc.0: If the claim is about 'all perpendicular pairs', then (다) is an example where it does not hold as it stands, so it is also reasonable to judge it false. But it is even better if you also say in what range it is true.
y-m-45-01.s.s3.prompt: Make two different lines px+qy+r=0 (p, q, r are integers) that are perpendicular to the line 2x+3y=6 and do not pass through the origin. A line whose coefficients are simply multiplied by 2 or 3 is the same line.
y-m-45-01.s.s3.hint.0: Find the slope of 2x+3y=6, and recall what relation the two slopes had in the perpendicular pairs (가) and (라) of the first problem.
y-m-45-01.s.s3.hint.1: Choose p and q of px+qy+r=0 so that the slope you found comes out, then choose r by trying values that do not pass through the origin.
y-m-45-01.s.s3.ok.c1: The coefficient of x is not 0.
y-m-45-01.s.s3.fail.c1: If the coefficient p of x is 0, it becomes a horizontal line and is not perpendicular to 2x+3y=6.
y-m-45-01.s.s3.fail.c2: It is not perpendicular to the given line. Compare the directions of the two lines.
y-m-45-01.s.s3.ok.c3: It does not pass through the origin.
y-m-45-01.s.s3.fail.c3: If r is 0, it passes through the origin.
y-m-45-01.s.s3.fail.c4: Please make p, q, r integers.
y-m-45-01.s.s3.explain: The slope of 2x+3y=6 is −2/3, so the slope of a perpendicular line is 3/2, and in coefficients (p, q) is a multiple of (3, −2). Examples: 3x−2y+1=0, 3x−2y−4=0. 6x−4y+2=0 is the same line as 3x−2y+1=0.
y-m-45-01.s.s3.because.prompt: Write how you chose p and q, and in one or two sentences write whether the same method also works for a vertical line like x=2.
y-m-45-01.s.s3.because.hint.0: Reread the values or equations you found in the earlier steps and recall why they turn out that way.
y-m-45-01.s.s3.because.hint.1: First write the reason that comes to mind as one sentence of the form '... so ...', then polish it.
y-m-45-01.s.s3.because.placeholder: Example: I chose p and q as ... A line like x=2 is ...
y-m-45-01.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write what value of 2x+3y=6 your chosen p and q are connected to?
y-m-45-01.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you think about where your method gets stuck for a line with no slope, like a vertical line?
y-m-45-01.s.s3.because.selfAssess.2: Did you think of another way of saying it that does not get stuck (a method that looks only at the coefficients)?
y-m-45-01.s.s3.because.model.0: The slope of 2x+3y=6 is −2/3, so the slope of the perpendicular line is 3/2, and I took the form 3x−2y+r=0. A vertical line like x=2 has no slope, so this method gets stuck, but you only need to look at the coefficients.
y-m-45-01.s.s3.because.model.1: I swapped the coefficients (2, 3) and changed the sign of one of them to get (3, −2). The vertical line x=2 and the horizontal line y=5 cannot be described by the product of slopes, but in a drawing they are perpendicular, so they must be thought about separately.

y-m-45-02.title: Where did 수빈's solution go wrong?
y-m-45-02.topic: Checking a solution for a perpendicular bisector of a segment, and points at equal distance
y-m-45-02.goal: Find the first line where the solution goes wrong, tell apart the checks that catch a wrong result from those that do not, and make points on the correct line yourself.
y-m-45-02.material: 수빈 wrote a solution to find the perpendicular bisector of segment AB joining the two points A(−1, 4) and B(5, 0) (the line that passes through the midpoint of segment AB and is perpendicular to AB). A point on the perpendicular bisector of segment AB is the same distance from A and B.
y-m-45-02.thinking.0: Finding where the error in the solution is
y-m-45-02.thinking.1: Comparing the power of checking methods
y-m-45-02.thinking.2: Making and checking the correct result yourself
y-m-45-02.prereq.0: The H2 of this task is only a difficulty level for production assignment and is not a grade assignment in the curriculum. Assume the learner has already studied middle-school linear functions (slope) and the Pythagorean theorem, and equations of lines in high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-45-02.prereq.1: Midpoint and slope of two points
y-m-45-02.prereq.2: Product of slopes and the perpendicular relation
y-m-45-02.prereq.3: Distance between points given by coordinates
y-m-45-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in 수빈's solution that goes wrong.
y-m-45-02.s.s1.hint.0: Tell apart the lines that simply take over the value from the previous line from the lines that use a new rule.
y-m-45-02.s.s1.hint.1: On the line where a new rule is used, actually multiply the two slopes.
y-m-45-02.s.s1.line.0: The midpoint of segment AB is ((−1+5)/2, (4+0)/2) = (2, 2).
y-m-45-02.s.s1.line.2: They are perpendicular, so the slope of the required line is the reciprocal of −2/3, which is −3/2.
y-m-45-02.s.s1.line.3: It passes through the point (2, 2), so y−2 = −3/2·(x−2), that is, 3x+2y−10=0.
y-m-45-02.s.s1.line.4: So the required perpendicular bisector is 3x+2y−10=0.
y-m-45-02.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is the first that goes wrong. The product of the slopes of two perpendicular lines is −1, so the slope that gives −1 when multiplied by −2/3 is 3/2. 수빈 took only the reciprocal and did not change the sign. The midpoint and slope in lines 1 and 2 are right, and lines 4 and 5 are also wrong because they use the value from line 3 as it is.
y-m-45-02.s.s2.o.a: Substitute the coordinates to check whether the midpoint (2, 2) of segment AB is on this line
y-m-45-02.s.s2.r.a: There are very many lines that merely pass through the midpoint. This check lets wrong lines pass too.
y-m-45-02.s.s2.o.c: Substitute the coordinates to check whether this line passes through point A or point B
y-m-45-02.s.s2.r.c: The perpendicular bisector does not pass through A or B. This check can hardly tell right from wrong.
y-m-45-02.s.s2.explain: Every point on the perpendicular bisector is the same distance from A and B. If you pick one point that is not the midpoint, for example (0, 5), the square of the distance to A is 2 and to B is 50, which are not equal, so it shows that this line is wrong.
y-m-45-02.s.s3.prompt: Make three different points P(x, y) on the correct perpendicular bisector. (They just need to be points at the same distance from A and B. The coordinates can be decimals.)
y-m-45-02.s.s3.hint.0: Think about how to write, using x and y, the condition that point P is the same distance from A and B.
y-m-45-02.s.s3.hint.1: Make the points one at a time by choosing x and then fitting y.
y-m-45-02.s.s3.ok.c1: It is the same distance from A and B.
y-m-45-02.s.s3.fail.c1: The distance to A and the distance to B are different. Calculate the squares of the distances and compare them.
y-m-45-02.s.s3.explain: The correct perpendicular bisector is 3x−2y−2=0. Points such as (2, 2), (0, −1), (4, 5), (−2, −4) are all on this line. On 수빈's line, the point (0, 5) has the square of the distance to A equal to 2 and to B equal to 50, so it does not satisfy the condition.

y-m-45-03.title: Where are the points at distance 2 from l?
y-m-45-03.topic: The set of points at a constant distance from a line
y-m-45-03.goal: Test with example points the idea that points at the same distance from a line lie on one line, and state the figure on which those points lie.
y-m-45-03.material: There is a line l: 3x+4y−10=0 ('3x plus 4y minus 10 equals 0'). 하윤 said, "The points at distance exactly 2 from l are on one line parallel to l." Distance is measured by the length of the perpendicular dropped from the point to the line.
y-m-45-03.thinking.0: Testing a claim with example points
y-m-45-03.thinking.1: Making a pair of points on opposite sides
y-m-45-03.thinking.2: Explaining the figure that the set of points forms
y-m-45-03.prereq.0: The H2 of this task is only a difficulty level for production assignment and is not a grade assignment in the curriculum. Assume the learner has already studied middle-school linear functions (slope) and the Pythagorean theorem, and equations of lines in high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-45-03.prereq.1: How to find the distance between a point and a line (first-year high school level)
y-m-45-03.prereq.2: The relation between two parallel lines
y-m-45-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the points below whose distance from the line l is 2.
y-m-45-03.s.s1.hint.0: First find the value you get by substituting the coordinates of each point into 3x+4y−10.
y-m-45-03.s.s1.hint.1: Using a point whose distance you already know, like the point (2, 1) on the line, check how the substituted value relates to the distance, and record the sign too.
y-m-45-03.s.s1.r.a: A point on the line has distance 0. Substitute into 3x+4y−10 and check the value.
y-m-45-03.s.s1.r.b: This is a point where the absolute value of the substituted value divided by 5 gives distance 2. Also look at which side the sign is on.
y-m-45-03.s.s1.r.c: The substituted value is 9, so the distance is 9/5. It is less than 2.
y-m-45-03.s.s1.r.d: This is a point where the absolute value of the substituted value divided by 5 gives distance 2. Also look at which side the sign is on.
y-m-45-03.s.s1.r.e: The substituted value is −16, so the distance is 16/5. It is more than 2.
y-m-45-03.s.s1.explain: The absolute value of 3x+4y−10 divided by 5 is the distance. For (0, 0) the value is −10 and for (4, 2) the value is +10, so both are at distance 2. But the signs differ, so they are on opposite sides of l.
y-m-45-03.s.s2.prompt: Make two different pairs of points P(x1, y1), Q(x2, y2) that are at distance 2 from l and on opposite sides of l. (P is on the side where 3x+4y>10, and Q is on the side where 3x+4y<10.)
y-m-45-03.s.s2.hint.0: Think about what value of 3x+4y−10 gives distance 2, splitting it into the two cases + and −.
y-m-45-03.s.s2.hint.1: Choose one point on one side, and on the opposite side make a point by fitting the value of 3x+4y differently.
y-m-45-03.s.s2.ok.c1: P is on the side of l where 3x+4y>10.
y-m-45-03.s.s2.fail.c1: P must be on the side where 3x+4y is greater than 10.
y-m-45-03.s.s2.ok.c2: Q is on the side of l where 3x+4y<10.
y-m-45-03.s.s2.fail.c2: Q must be on the side where 3x+4y is less than 10.
y-m-45-03.s.s2.ok.c3: The distance from P to l is 2.
y-m-45-03.s.s2.fail.c3: The distance from P to l is not 2. Check the value of 3x+4y−10.
y-m-45-03.s.s2.ok.c4: The distance from Q to l is 2.
y-m-45-03.s.s2.fail.c4: The distance from Q to l is not 2. Check the value of 3x+4y−10.
y-m-45-03.s.s2.explain: Points on 3x+4y=20 such as (4, 2), (0, 5), (8, −1) are at distance 2 on one side of l, and points on 3x+4y=0 such as (0, 0), (4, −3), (−4, 3) are at distance 2 on the opposite side.
y-m-45-03.s.s2.because.prompt: Write your judgment of 하윤's claim based on the positions of the points. What figure do the points at distance 2 lie on?
y-m-45-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: Reread the value or equation you found in the earlier step and recall why it turns out that way.
y-m-45-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: First write the reason that comes to mind as one sentence of the form '... so ...', then polish it.
y-m-45-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you connect the fact that the pair of points you made are on opposite sides to your judgment of the claim?
y-m-45-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say that both lines are parallel to l?
y-m-45-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you show it concretely using equations like 3x+4y=20 and 3x+4y=0?
y-m-45-03.s.s2.because.model.0: 하윤's statement is only half right. The points at distance 2 lie on two lines parallel to l, one on each side of l. 3x+4y=20 and 3x+4y=0 are those equations.
y-m-45-03.s.s2.because.model.1: It is not just one line. The points (4, 2) and (0, 0) have the same distance but are on opposite sides of l, so they lie on two lines parallel to l, one each.
y-m-45-03.s.s3.prompt: You want to fix 하윤's statement. Which of the following sentences fits best?
y-m-45-03.s.s3.hint.0: Join the two points you chose in s1 and compare how the direction of the segment (0, 0)-(4, 2) relates to l.
y-m-45-03.s.s3.hint.1: Say where the points of equal distance are by splitting into the left (lower) and right (upper) of l.
y-m-45-03.s.s3.o.a: The points at distance 2 from l lie on two lines parallel to l
y-m-45-03.s.s3.r.a: This sentence shows that there is one on each side of l.
y-m-45-03.s.s3.o.b: The points at distance 2 from l lie on a line perpendicular to l that passes through the origin
y-m-45-03.s.s3.r.b: Points on a perpendicular line are at various distances from l. Check whether (0, 0) and (4, 2) are on one perpendicular line.
y-m-45-03.s.s3.o.c: The points at distance 2 from l lie on a circle of radius 2 centered at a point on l
y-m-45-03.s.s3.r.c: A point on the circle can be at a distance less than 2 from l. Work out the distance from a point on the circle to l.
y-m-45-03.s.s3.o.d: The points at distance 2 from l all lie on only one line parallel to l
y-m-45-03.s.s3.r.d: Check whether (0, 0) and (4, 2) are on one line, and whether it is parallel to l.
y-m-45-03.s.s3.explain: There is one line parallel to l at distance 2 from l on each side of l, so the points at distance 2 lie on two lines.

y-m-45-04.title: What must be given to determine a circle uniquely?
y-m-45-04.topic: Conditions that determine the equation of a circle uniquely, and missing conditions
y-m-45-04.goal: Judge whether a set of given conditions determines a circle uniquely, and when conditions are missing, make different circles that satisfy the conditions yourself and say what more is needed.
y-m-45-04.material: You want to determine one circle on a coordinate plane. For each set of conditions below, you want to find out whether there is 'exactly one circle that satisfies all the conditions'. (x² is read 'x squared', and (x−a)² is read 'x minus a, squared'.)
y-m-45-04.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
y-m-45-04.thinking.1: Showing the insufficiency with two different circles
y-m-45-04.prereq.0: The H2 of this task is only a difficulty level for production assignment and is not a grade assignment in the curriculum. Assume the learner has already studied middle-school linear functions (slope) and the Pythagorean theorem, and equations of lines in high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-45-04.prereq.1: Equation of a circle (x−a)²+(y−b)²=r² (a, b is the center, r is the radius)
y-m-45-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the sets for which there is exactly one circle satisfying all the conditions.
y-m-45-04.s.s1.hint.0: Count how many values you need to find in the circle equation (x−a)²+(y−b)²=r², and how many of them each condition determines.
y-m-45-04.s.s1.hint.1: For a set where some value is left undetermined by the conditions, test which value you can change while the conditions still hold.
y-m-45-04.s.s1.o.a: It passes through the one point (2, 1) and the radius is 5
y-m-45-04.s.s1.r.a: The point and the radius alone do not determine the center. Every place at distance 5 from the point is a candidate for the center.
y-m-45-04.s.s1.o.b: The center is (1, 2) and the radius is 3
y-m-45-04.s.s1.r.b: With the center and radius the equation is determined right away. This is the case where all the unknowns a, b, r are given.
y-m-45-04.s.s1.o.c: It is tangent to both the x-axis and the y-axis and passes through the point (2, 1)
y-m-45-04.s.s1.r.c: In the tangency conditions, check how many solutions the quadratic equation for finding r has.
y-m-45-04.s.s1.o.d: The center is on the x-axis and it passes through the two points (1, 2), (1, −2)
y-m-45-04.s.s1.r.d: The two points are symmetric about the x-axis, so a center at the same distance from both points can be anywhere on the x-axis.
y-m-45-04.s.s1.o.e: The two ends of a diameter are (−1, 3), (5, 1)
y-m-45-04.s.s1.r.e: With the two endpoints, the center is determined as the midpoint and the radius as the distance to an endpoint.
y-m-45-04.s.s1.o.f: The center is on the x-axis and it passes through the two points (1, 2), (5, 2)
y-m-45-04.s.s1.r.f: This is a condition for finding a point on the x-axis at the same distance from the two points. Work out how many such points there are.
y-m-45-04.s.s1.explain: In b the center and radius are given. In e the center is the midpoint (2, 2) and the radius is half the distance between the two endpoints. In f the x-coordinate of the center is fixed at 3, the middle of the two points, so the center (3, 0) is determined uniquely. In a there are infinitely many centers, in c there are two circles with radius 1 and radius 5, and in d the h of the center (h, 0) is free, so there are infinitely many circles.
y-m-45-04.s.s2.prompt: In set c), make two different circles that satisfy the conditions. The point (2, 1) is in the first quadrant, so the center (a, b) is also in the first quadrant, and if it is tangent to both axes, a=b=r.
y-m-45-04.s.s2.hint.0: Put a=b=r into the equation for passing through the point so that only r is left, and find what values r can take.
y-m-45-04.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the number of circles differs depending on whether the equation for r has one solution or two.
y-m-45-04.s.s2.fail.c1: The radius must be greater than 0.
y-m-45-04.s.s2.ok.c2: It is tangent to both the x-axis and the y-axis (first quadrant).
y-m-45-04.s.s2.fail.c2: To be tangent to both axes, the coordinates of the center must equal the radius.
y-m-45-04.s.s2.fail.c3: Check whether the square of the distance from the point (2, 1) to the center equals r².
y-m-45-04.s.s2.explain: Simplifying (r−2)²+(r−1)²=r² gives r²−6r+5=0, so r=1 or r=5. So both circles (x−1)²+(y−1)²=1 and (x−5)²+(y−5)²=25 satisfy the conditions.
y-m-45-04.s.s3.prompt: Write why there are two circles in set c), and write what more information would be needed for the circle to be determined uniquely.
y-m-45-04.s.s3.hint.0: Compare the radii of the two circles you made in set c and look at what differs.
y-m-45-04.s.s3.hint.1: Think about which value, such as the center or the radius, can separate the two circles.
y-m-45-04.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The solutions of the equation for r are ... so if we also know ...
y-m-45-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write the equation for r and give the fact that it has two solutions as your reason?
y-m-45-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check that the extra information you gave (radius, center, etc.) actually lets you choose one of the two circles?
y-m-45-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you check that adding just one more piece of information is enough to determine it?
y-m-45-04.s.s3.model.0: The quadratic equation r²−6r+5=0 for r has two solutions, 1 and 5, so there are two circles. If we are told whether the radius is 1 or 5, it is determined uniquely.
y-m-45-04.s.s3.model.1: Under the condition of passing through the point (2, 1), both r=1 and r=5 are possible. If we know one more piece of information such as the center or the radius, it becomes just one.

y-m-45-05.title: When does a line moved upward come off the circle?
y-m-45-05.topic: The positions of a circle and a line, and the moment of tangency
y-m-45-05.goal: Use data to predict how the number of points where a line meets a circle changes as the y-intercept grows, and revise a guess about the moment of tangency into a calculation.
y-m-45-05.material: Consider the circle C: x²+y²=25 (center at the origin, radius 5) and the line y=x+k. k is the y-intercept and the slope is 1. Increase k gradually from 0, moving the line upward, and investigate the number of points where the line and the circle meet. (√2 is read 'root 2' and is about 1.414.)
y-m-45-05.thinking.0: Revising a prediction with step-by-step data
y-m-45-05.prereq.0: The H2 of this task is only a difficulty level for production assignment and is not a grade assignment in the curriculum. Assume the learner has already studied middle-school linear functions (slope) and the Pythagorean theorem, and equations of lines in high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-45-05.prereq.1: The equation of a circle x²+y²=r²
y-m-45-05.prereq.2: Equation of a line and simultaneous quadratic equations
y-m-45-05.prereq.3: The meaning of the discriminant of a quadratic equation
y-m-45-05.s.s1.prompt: The data is revealed one piece at a time. At each step, choose a prediction and revise it with the next data.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, compare whether the newly revealed data conflicts with the earlier prediction or not.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.hint.1: Pick one k and substitute it directly into x²+(x+k)²=25 to check the number of points.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.0.info: If k=0, the line is y=x and passes through the center of the circle. It meets the circle at two different points.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.0.ask: As you increase k gradually from 0, what do you think happens to the number of points where they meet?
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.0.after: The k=0 data alone cannot tell when the moment of tangency is. Both a and c are predictions worth testing.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It stays 2 for a while, then at some moment becomes 1 (tangent), and after that becomes 0
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.0.r.a: It is the right direction that a moment of tangency occurs. We do not yet know when that moment is.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.0.o.b: As soon as k becomes even slightly positive it immediately becomes 1, and after that it stays 0
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.0.r.b: The line that was passing through the center has only moved a little. It has not gone far enough to be tangent right away.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It is tangent at k=5 (when the y-intercept equals the radius), and after that it becomes 0
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is the idea that it is tangent when the y-intercept equals the radius. It is a guess worth testing.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It is always 2, regardless of k
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This would mean that even when the line goes very far up it still meets the circle. Recall that the circle lies in a small region.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.1.info: Test k=5. Putting y=x+5 into x²+y²=25 gives x²+(x+5)²=25, that is, 2x²+10x=0, so x=0 or x=−5. The points where they meet are the two points (0, 5) and (−5, 0).
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.1.ask: At k=5 the line was not tangent and met the circle at two points. Which is the fitting judgment about the positive value of k at which it becomes tangent?
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.1.after: Even though the y-intercept equals the radius 5, it was not tangent. The slope is 1, so the line meets the circle at a slant, and the moment of tangency happens higher up.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It becomes tangent at a value less than 5
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.1.r.a: If it were tangent at a k less than 5, then at k=5 it should already not meet. But at k=5 it met at two points.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It is tangent at 5. The calculation must be wrong
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Check the calculation again. (0, 5) and (−5, 0) are both points on the circle.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It becomes tangent at a value greater than 5
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.1.r.c: At k=5 there are still two points, so the moment of tangency appears higher up than that.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.1.o.d: There is no k at which it is tangent
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.1.r.d: The circle has a finite size, so if the line goes up far enough it will no longer meet it. Then there is a moment of tangency in between.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.2.info: Test k=7. x²+(x+7)²=25 is 2x²+14x+24=0, so x=−3 or x=−4. The points where they meet are (−3, 4) and (−4, 3), still two.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.2.ask: Which is the fitting judgment about the number of meeting points when k=8?
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.2.after: Whether it is 2 or 0 depends on whether the k at which it is tangent is greater or less than 8. So let's calculate in general.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It cannot be decided with the data so far, because we do not know whether the tangent k is greater or less than 8
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This judgment pins down the limit of the data precisely.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It will be 2, because the tangent k may be greater than 8
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Up to k=7 there are two points, so that could be. But it is not settled.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.2.o.c: It will be exactly 1, because one can guess by pattern that the tangent k happens to be 8
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.2.r.c: There is no evidence in the data that the tangent value is 8. This assumes a case that happens to be right.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.2.o.d: It will be 0, because the tangent k may be between 7 and 8
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Up to k=7 there are two points, so that could be. But it is not settled.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.3.info: Putting y=x+k into the equation of the circle gives 2x²+2kx+k²−25=0, and one fourth of the discriminant of this equation is k²−2(k²−25)=50−k². If this value is positive there are two points, if 0 it is tangent, and if negative they do not meet. The square root of 50, 5√2, is about 7.07.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.3.ask: What is the range of k for which the line meets the circle at two different points?
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.3.after: The moment of tangency happens at k=5√2 (about 7.07) and k=−5√2. At k=8 there are 0 points. The first guess, 'it is tangent when the y-intercept equals the radius', was wrong because the slope of the line is 1.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.3.r.a: This is the range where the value of the discriminant is positive.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.3.r.b: They also met at two points at k=5 and k=7. Test the guess that 5 is the end.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.3.r.c: k=7 gave two points, but 7.05 can also give two points. Find the end exactly.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.3.o.d: All k with k<5√2 (including very small negative numbers)
y-m-45-05.s.s1.st.3.r.d: Think about the case where k is a very small negative number. The line is far below the circle.
y-m-45-05.s.s1.reflect: If at first you guessed that it would be tangent at k=5, how did the data showing two points at k=5 change that guess? What prediction did the data showing two points at k=7 make possible, and what prediction did it leave open? Tell apart waiting for hidden information from checking a guess by calculation.
y-m-45-05.s.s2.prompt: Instead of the discriminant, you can also find the same range by 'comparing the distance from the center of the circle to the line with the radius'. The distance from the center (0, 0) to the line x−y+k=0 is |k|/√2. What is the fitting comparison?
y-m-45-05.s.s2.hint.0: First compare the distance from the center to the line and the number of meeting points when k=0.
y-m-45-05.s.s2.hint.1: Estimate the value of |k|/√2 when k=8 and compare it with 5.
y-m-45-05.s.s2.o.a: If the distance |k|/√2 is greater than 5 they meet at two points, if equal they are tangent, and if less they do not meet
y-m-45-05.s.s2.r.a: When the distance is far, the line moves away from the circle. 'Greater' and 'less' are reversed.
y-m-45-05.s.s2.o.b: Regard the distance from the center to the line as k itself, and judge that it is tangent at the moment k equals 5
y-m-45-05.s.s2.r.b: k is only the y-intercept, not the length of the perpendicular from the center to the line. When the slope is 1, the length of the perpendicular is different.
y-m-45-05.s.s2.o.c: If the distance |k|/√2 is less than 5 they meet at two points, if equal they are tangent, and if greater they do not meet
y-m-45-05.s.s2.r.c: Comparing the distance with the radius gives the same conclusion. The idea is that if it is near they meet, and if it is far they do not meet.
y-m-45-05.s.s2.o.d: The formula for the distance can be used only where there is no circle, so for a circle only the discriminant can be used
y-m-45-05.s.s2.r.d: There is a formula for the distance between a point and a line, so you can use the distance.
y-m-45-05.s.s2.explain: If the distance |k|/√2 is less than the radius 5, they meet at two points. |k|<5√2, so it is the same as −5√2<k<5√2 found with the discriminant. The two methods agree.

y-m-45-06.title: Is checking with one set of numbers a proof?
y-m-45-06.topic: How to place coordinates, and generality, when showing a property of a figure with coordinates
y-m-45-06.goal: When showing a property of a figure with coordinates, sort out which coordinate setup represents every triangle, and explain to a friend why a solution that uses one special figure is not a proof.
y-m-45-06.material: Let M and N be the midpoints of the two sides AB and AC of triangle ABC. You want to show with coordinates that segment MN is parallel to side BC and its length is half of BC. (√3 is read 'root 3'.) How you place the coordinates matters.
y-m-45-06.thinking.0: Choosing a coordinate setup that does not lose generality
y-m-45-06.thinking.1: Finding the error of generalizing in a solution
y-m-45-06.thinking.2: Fixing and explaining it to a friend in suitable words
y-m-45-06.prereq.0: The H2 of this task is only a difficulty level for production assignment and is not a grade assignment in the curriculum. Assume the learner has already studied middle-school linear functions (slope) and the Pythagorean theorem, and equations of lines in high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-45-06.prereq.1: Midpoint, slope, and distance between two points
y-m-45-06.prereq.2: The property of the segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle (a known result at the middle-school level)
y-m-45-06.s.s1.prompt: You want to show this fact 'for any triangle ABC'. Choose all the coordinate setups that can represent every triangle (that do not lose generality). (a, b, c are letters that do not restrict the shape, such as being positive numbers.)
y-m-45-06.s.s1.hint.0: For each setup, look at the kinds of triangles you can make by changing the coordinates of the vertices (changing the letters or the numbers).
y-m-45-06.s.s1.hint.1: With the same setup, test whether you can make a right triangle, an equilateral triangle, and any shape.
y-m-45-06.s.s1.o.a: A(0, 0), B(4, 0), C(0, 3)  (all coordinates are numbers)
y-m-45-06.s.s1.r.a: It is fixed by numbers, so it shows only one right triangle.
y-m-45-06.s.s1.r.b: If you put one side on the x-axis and one vertex at the origin, the remaining vertex is free, so it can show any triangle.
y-m-45-06.s.s1.r.c: It fixes the x-coordinate of A at 0, so it shows only triangles with a right angle at B.
y-m-45-06.s.s1.o.d: A(0, 0), B(2, 0), C(1, √3)  (all coordinates are fixed)
y-m-45-06.s.s1.r.d: It shows only one equilateral triangle in which all three sides are 2.
y-m-45-06.s.s1.r.e: This is the method of putting the midpoint of side BC at the origin. A is free, so it can show any triangle.
y-m-45-06.s.s1.r.f: It puts A on the perpendicular bisector of side BC, so it shows only isosceles triangles.
y-m-45-06.s.s1.explain: You can translate and rotate the triangle to put one side on the x-axis (flipping it if needed so that A is above the x-axis) and put one vertex at the origin, or put the midpoint of that side at the origin. Lengths and parallel relations do not change when moving, so b and e represent every triangle. a, c, d, f show only triangles whose shape is already fixed, such as a right triangle, an equilateral triangle, or an isosceles triangle.
y-m-45-06.s.s2.prompt: A student placed A(0, 0), B(4, 0), C(0, 3) and wrote as below. Choose the line that is a problem as a proof. (You may choose just one line.)
y-m-45-06.s.s2.hint.0: Recalculate the calculations in lines 2 to 4 one by one to see whether they are right for this triangle.
y-m-45-06.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the kinds of triangles that can be made from the coordinates in line 1 with the range that line 5 talks about.
y-m-45-06.s.s2.line.0: Place the vertices of triangle ABC as A(0, 0), B(4, 0), C(0, 3).
y-m-45-06.s.s2.line.1: The midpoint M of AB is (2, 0), and the midpoint N of AC is (0, 3/2).
y-m-45-06.s.s2.line.2: The slope of MN is (3/2−0)/(0−2)=−3/4 and the slope of BC is (3−0)/(0−4)=−3/4, so MN and BC are parallel.
y-m-45-06.s.s2.line.3: MN=√(2²+(3/2)²)=5/2 and BC=√(4²+3²)=5, so MN is half of BC.
y-m-45-06.s.s2.line.4: Therefore, in every triangle, the segment joining the midpoints of two sides is parallel to the remaining side and its length is half of it.
y-m-45-06.s.s2.explain: Lines 1 and 5 are the problem. The calculations (lines 2 to 4) are all right, but because line 1 fixed the coordinates with one right triangle, you cannot move on to 'every triangle' in line 5. The only thing checked is this one triangle.
y-m-45-06.s.s3.prompt: Tell the friend who wrote this solution why it is not a proof for every triangle, and write in two or three sentences how to fix it. Write in words that are easy for your friend to understand.
y-m-45-06.s.s3.hint.0: Imagine you are explaining to your friend, and first say what kind of triangle this solution dealt with.
y-m-45-06.s.s3.hint.1: Recall how you should write the coordinates to include triangles of other shapes too.
y-m-45-06.s.s3.placeholder: Example: This solution is ... so ... To fix it ...
y-m-45-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write the reason in concrete words so your friend can understand?
y-m-45-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say 'it does not represent every triangle' rather than 'the calculation is wrong'?
y-m-45-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you check that your way of fixing it really includes every triangle?
y-m-45-06.s.s3.model.0: A(0,0), B(4,0), C(0,3) is just one right triangle. We cannot tell whether it works for other triangles too. You should place it with letters like B(0,0), C(c,0), A(a,b) and do the same calculation.
y-m-45-06.s.s3.model.1: If you check with only one set of numbers, you haven't tried the cases that are not right triangles. You have to show it again with the vertex coordinates as any numbers a, b, c so that it can be any triangle.

y-m-45-07.title: If the point that is always passed through as k changes is (1, 2), do all the lines come out?
y-m-45-07.topic: Points that a line depending on k always passes through, and points it does not pass through
y-m-45-07.goal: Find the error in the process of finding the fixed point in a solution, sort out valid ways to check the fixed point, and test the idea that 'the family contains every line through the fixed point' by finding a point the family of lines does not pass through.
y-m-45-07.material: For a real number k, consider the line l_k: (k+1)x+(k−2)y−3k+3=0 ('k plus 1 times x, plus k minus 2 times y, minus 3k plus 3 equals 0'). The point that it always passes through whatever the value of k is (1, 2). 민아 said, "Any line that passes through the point (1, 2) can be made as l_k by choosing k suitably."
y-m-45-07.thinking.0: Finding the error in a solution
y-m-45-07.thinking.1: Judging whether a checking method is sufficient
y-m-45-07.thinking.2: Making a point that is a counterexample yourself
y-m-45-07.prereq.0: The H2 of this task is only a difficulty level for production assignment and is not a grade assignment in the curriculum. Assume the learner has already studied middle-school linear functions (slope) and the Pythagorean theorem, and equations of lines in high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-45-07.prereq.1: Equation of a line and the intersection of two lines
y-m-45-07.prereq.2: The meaning of an identity in k (an expression that holds regardless of the value of k)
y-m-45-07.s.s1.prompt: A student solved it as below to find the fixed point. Choose the first line that goes wrong.
y-m-45-07.s.s1.hint.0: Pick one of the two equations from line 2, put in the y from line 3 directly, and recalculate x.
y-m-45-07.s.s1.hint.1: Substitute the point in line 5 into both equations from line 2 and check whether they hold.
y-m-45-07.s.s1.line.0: Arranging (k+1)x+(k−2)y−3k+3=0 in terms of k gives k(x+y−3)+(x−2y+3)=0.
y-m-45-07.s.s1.line.1: For it to hold regardless of the value of k, we need x+y−3=0 and x−2y+3=0.
y-m-45-07.s.s1.line.2: Subtracting the two equations side by side gives 3y−6=0, so y=2.
y-m-45-07.s.s1.line.3: Putting y=2 into x+y−3=0 gives x=−1.
y-m-45-07.s.s1.explain: Line 4 goes wrong. Putting y=2 into x+y−3=0 gives x+2−3=0, so x=1. Writing x=−1 is a sign error, and line 5 is the result of taking that value as it is. Even putting (−1, 2) into x−2y+3=0 gives −1−4+3≠0, so it does not satisfy both equations.
y-m-45-07.s.s2.prompt: Suppose the candidate for the fixed point is (1, 2). Choose all the checking methods that are enough to confirm that this point is on l_k 'for every k'. (The equation of l_k is a first-degree expression in k.)
y-m-45-07.s.s2.hint.0: Look at whether what remains when you put in (1, 2) is an expression in k or a number.
y-m-45-07.s.s2.hint.1: Compare whether the values of k you checked are only one, two or more different values, or whether you handled all k at once.
y-m-45-07.s.s2.o.a: Substituting (1, 2) into the one line for k=0 and checking that it passes through is enough
y-m-45-07.s.s2.r.a: A point being on one line does not mean it is on every line. Test what happens for other values of k.
y-m-45-07.s.s2.o.b: Substitute (1, 2) into the two lines for k=0 and k=1 to check (a first-degree expression in k)
y-m-45-07.s.s2.r.b: If you regard the value of the expression as a first-degree expression in k, then if it is 0 for two different values of k, it is 0 for every k.
y-m-45-07.s.s2.o.c: Substitute (1, 2) into the one line with a large value like k=100 to check
y-m-45-07.s.s2.r.c: Even if you take a large value of k, you have only checked one line. You cannot know whether it passes through for other k.
y-m-45-07.s.s2.o.d: Simplify the expression after substituting (1, 2) and check that it is 0 regardless of k
y-m-45-07.s.s2.r.d: This is the method of regarding the substituted value as an expression in k and seeing whether the coefficient of k and the remainder are both 0.
y-m-45-07.s.s2.explain: Substituting (1, 2) gives (k+1)+2(k−2)−3k+3=0, which holds regardless of k. Checking with general k like this (d) is the most direct, and because the expression is first-degree in k, checking that it is 0 at two different values (k=0, 1) (b) is also enough. Checking only one value (a, c) is only a check of that one line.
y-m-45-07.s.s3.prompt: Among the points (x, y) other than the point (1, 2), find two different points that l_k does not pass through whichever k you choose. (If such points exist, what happens to 민아's statement?)
y-m-45-07.s.s3.hint.0: Put (x, y) into the equation of l_k and arrange it as an expression in k. Think about when there is no k at all that satisfies that expression.
y-m-45-07.s.s3.hint.1: First find the points where the part multiplied by k becomes 0.
y-m-45-07.s.s3.ok.c1: The coefficient of k, x+y−3, in the equation of this family of lines becomes 0.
y-m-45-07.s.s3.fail.c1: Check whether the coefficient of k becomes 0 when you put (x, y) into the equation.
y-m-45-07.s.s3.ok.c2: It is not the fixed point (1, 2).
y-m-45-07.s.s3.fail.c2: If the x-coordinate is 1, it becomes the fixed point (1, 2).
y-m-45-07.s.s3.explain: Substituting (x, y) gives k(x+y−3)+(x−2y+3)=0. For it to hold for no k, the coefficient of k, x+y−3, must be 0 while the remainder x−2y+3 is not 0. This is true of points with x+y=3 other than (1, 2). Examples: (3, 0), (0, 3), (4, −1). So the line x+y=3 through (1, 2) is not among the l_k.
y-m-45-07.s.s3.because.prompt: Write in one sentence the rule on which the points you found lie, and explain why that rule leads to 'it does not pass through whichever k you choose'.
y-m-45-07.s.s3.because.hint.0: Reread the value or equation you found in the earlier step and recall why it turns out that way.
y-m-45-07.s.s3.because.hint.1: First write the reason that comes to mind as one sentence of the form '... so ...', then polish it.
y-m-45-07.s.s3.because.placeholder: Example: The points I found are ... Because ...
y-m-45-07.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write the rule as an equation?
y-m-45-07.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say that this equation is the same as the condition that the coefficient of k becomes 0 when substituted?
y-m-45-07.s.s3.because.selfAssess.2: Did you check that the remaining part is not 0, so it cannot be matched with any k?
y-m-45-07.s.s3.because.model.0: All the points are on x+y=3. When substituted, the coefficient x+y−3 in front of k becomes 0 so k disappears, and the remaining x−2y+3 is not 0, so it cannot be matched with any k.
y-m-45-07.s.s3.because.model.1: Adding the x-coordinate and y-coordinate of the point gives 3. Then the term multiplied by k becomes 0, so the value does not change even if k changes, and the remainder is not 0, so the equation does not hold.

y-m-45-08.title: If you change the order of the moves, is the result the same?
y-m-45-08.topic: The order when combining a translation and a reflection
y-m-45-08.goal: Find the error in a solution about moving a line, and find and generalize the condition under which changing the order of a translation and a reflection across the line y=x gives the same result.
y-m-45-08.material: You want to move the line m: y=2x+1 twice. Move ㉠ is a translation by 3 in the x direction (3 to the right), and move ㉡ is a reflection across the line y=x. 지후 did ㉠ first and then ㉡.
y-m-45-08.thinking.0: Finding the error in a solution
y-m-45-08.thinking.1: Making cases where the order can be swapped
y-m-45-08.thinking.2: Generalizing the condition in one sentence
y-m-45-08.prereq.0: The H2 of this task is only a difficulty level for production assignment and is not a grade assignment in the curriculum. Assume the learner has already studied middle-school linear functions (slope) and the Pythagorean theorem, and equations of lines in high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-45-08.prereq.1: Translating a figure (replacing x with x−a and y with y−b)
y-m-45-08.prereq.2: Reflection across the line y=x means swapping x and y
y-m-45-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in 지후's solution that goes wrong.
y-m-45-08.s.s1.hint.0: Pick one point on the translated line and work backward to see which point on the original line it was moved from.
y-m-45-08.s.s1.hint.1: Put the point (0, 1) on m into the equation of the new line to check where it goes when moved 3 to the right.
y-m-45-08.s.s1.line.0: To translate m by 3 in the x direction, put x+3 in place of x: y=2(x+3)+1=2x+7.
y-m-45-08.s.s1.line.1: To reflect this line across y=x, swap x and y: x=2y+7.
y-m-45-08.s.s1.line.3: So the result of doing ㉠ and then ㉡ is y=(x−7)/2.
y-m-45-08.s.s1.explain: Line 1 goes wrong. When moved 3 to the right, a point (x, y) on the original graph goes to (x+3, y), so the equation of the new line is found by putting x−3 in place of x: y=2(x−3)+1=2x−5. The lines after that use the value from line 1 as it is. The correct result is y=(x+5)/2 from x=2y−5.
y-m-45-08.s.s2.prompt: This time, think about the point (1, 3). Find three different (p, q) for which the point you get by translating the point (1, 3) by (p, q) and then reflecting across y=x is the same as the point you get by first reflecting across y=x and then translating by (p, q). Leave out (0, 0). The coordinates (p, q) mean moving p in the x direction and q in the y direction.
y-m-45-08.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate the path of the point (1, 3) separately for each order, and write the coordinates of the final point using p and q.
y-m-45-08.s.s2.hint.1: Set the x-coordinates of the two final points equal and the y-coordinates equal, and see what relation arises between p and q.
y-m-45-08.s.s2.var.p: Move p in the x direction
y-m-45-08.s.s2.var.q: Move q in the y direction
y-m-45-08.s.s2.ok.c1: The results of the two orders are the same point.
y-m-45-08.s.s2.fail.c1: Find the coordinates of the point moved in each of the two orders and compare the x-coordinates with each other and the y-coordinates with each other.
y-m-45-08.s.s2.ok.c2: It is not (0, 0), which has no move.
y-m-45-08.s.s2.fail.c2: Leave out (0, 0) because there is no move.
y-m-45-08.s.s2.explain: For a translation followed by a reflection, (1+p, 3+q) goes to (3+q, 1+p), and for a reflection followed by a translation, (3, 1) goes to (3+p, 1+q). For the two points to be the same, 3+q=3+p and 1+p=1+q, so p=q. Examples: (1, 1), (2, 2), (−3, −3).
y-m-45-08.s.s2.because.prompt: Write what the (p, q) you found have in common, and explain in one or two sentences why the result is the same even when you swap the order in that relation.
y-m-45-08.s.s2.because.hint.0: Reread the value or equation you found in the earlier step and recall why it turns out that way.
y-m-45-08.s.s2.because.hint.1: First write the reason that comes to mind as one sentence of the form '... so ...', then polish it.
y-m-45-08.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: The (p, q) I found are all ... Because ...
y-m-45-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write the rule that the (p, q) you found have in common as an equation?
y-m-45-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you explain the reason using the fact that the reflection swaps the x-coordinate and the y-coordinate?
y-m-45-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you check that when p≠q the result differs depending on the order?
y-m-45-08.s.s2.because.model.0: p and q are the same (p=q). Reflecting across y=x swaps the x-coordinate and the y-coordinate, but if the amounts moved are the same, swapping gives the same thing, so the order does not matter.
y-m-45-08.s.s2.because.model.1: Like (1,1), (2,2), (−3,−3), it goes as much vertically as it goes horizontally. The reflection swaps x and y, and if the amounts moved in the two directions are equal, swapping gives the same, so the result is the same.
y-m-45-08.s.s3.prompt: Which is the most fitting statement that generalizes the result of s2 to figures (graphs)? (This is the case of moving a whole graph, not just one point.)
y-m-45-08.s.s3.hint.0: Split into the cases p=q and p≠q, and compare whether one point on the graph goes to the same place in the two orders.
y-m-45-08.s.s3.hint.1: Move the point (t, −t+c) on the line y=−x+c in the two orders.
y-m-45-08.s.s3.o.a: Sometimes the graphs are the same and sometimes different, and if p=q they are always the same
y-m-45-08.s.s3.r.a: If the results of moving the points are the same, the graphs are the same too. When p≠q, they may be the same depending on the graph.
y-m-45-08.s.s3.o.b: In the case of reflecting across y=x, swapping the order with a translation always gives the same result
y-m-45-08.s.s3.r.b: Testing with p=1, q=2 at the point (1, 3) gives different results. It is not always the same.
y-m-45-08.s.s3.o.c: Once the direction of the translation is fixed, swapping the order does not change anything
y-m-45-08.s.s3.r.c: Being given a direction does not make them the same. You have to look at the relation between the amounts p and q.
y-m-45-08.s.s3.o.d: If p≠q, the result of swapping the order is always different, whatever graph you move
y-m-45-08.s.s3.r.d: Depending on the graph, the result may be the same. Move the line y=−x+c in the two orders.
y-m-45-08.s.s3.explain: If p=q, the result of the two orders is the same at every point, so the graphs are the same too. If p≠q, they are usually different, but there is an exception: the line y=−x+c becomes the same line y=−x+c+p+q whichever order you move it in.

y-m-45-09.title: Is there only one point that gives the largest value in the region?
y-m-45-09.topic: The point with the largest value in the region shown by a system of inequalities
y-m-45-09.goal: After comparing values at the vertices of the region, show with example points that more than one point can give the maximum, and explain why.
y-m-45-09.material: Region D is the set of points (x, y) that satisfy all of x≥0, y≥0, x+y≤4, x+2y≤6. (Read: x is greater than or equal to 0, y is greater than or equal to 0, x plus y is less than or equal to 4, and x plus 2y is less than or equal to 6.) The vertices of D are (0, 0), (4, 0), (2, 2), (0, 3). Among the points (x, y) in D, find the points that make the value f=2x+2y the largest.
y-m-45-09.thinking.0: Comparing values at the vertices to choose candidates for the maximum
y-m-45-09.thinking.1: Making many points that satisfy the conditions
y-m-45-09.thinking.2: Explaining why it is not one point
y-m-45-09.prereq.0: The H2 of this task is only a difficulty level for production assignment and is not a grade assignment in the curriculum. Assume the learner has already studied middle-school linear functions (slope) and the Pythagorean theorem, and equations of lines in high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-45-09.prereq.1: The region shown by a system of linear inequalities (telling the boundary lines and the region)
y-m-45-09.s.s1.prompt: When you find the value of f=2x+2y at the four vertices, which explanation of the maximum is right?
y-m-45-09.s.s1.hint.0: Put the coordinates of the four vertices into the expression for f one at a time and arrange the values in a table.
y-m-45-09.s.s1.hint.1: Look at whether the vertex with the largest value is one or two or more.
y-m-45-09.s.s1.o.a: The maximum 8 occurs only at (4, 0), and all the other vertices are smaller
y-m-45-09.s.s1.o.b: (4, 0) and (2, 2) are both 8 and are the largest
y-m-45-09.s.s1.r.b: This is the way of finding and comparing the values at the two vertices.
y-m-45-09.s.s1.o.c: The maximum 8 occurs only at (2, 2), and all the other vertices are smaller
y-m-45-09.s.s1.o.d: The maximum occurs at (0, 3), and all the other vertices are smaller
y-m-45-09.s.s1.r.d: The value at (0, 3) is 6. Compare it with the values at the other vertices.
y-m-45-09.s.s1.explain: f is 0 at (0, 0), 8 at (4, 0), 8 at (2, 2), and 6 at (0, 3). Among the vertices, there are two points that give the maximum 8.
y-m-45-09.s.s2.prompt: Find three different points (x, y) that are in D and have f=2x+2y equal to 8. (Decimal coordinates are fine.)
y-m-45-09.s.s2.hint.0: Write what kind of line 2x+2y=8 is, and find the stretch on this line that satisfies all the inequalities of region D.
y-m-45-09.s.s2.hint.1: Check which vertices are at the two ends of that stretch, and then pick a point between them.
y-m-45-09.s.s2.fail.c1: x and y must be greater than or equal to 0.
y-m-45-09.s.s2.fail.c2: x+y is greater than 4. It is outside the region.
y-m-45-09.s.s2.fail.c3: x+2y is greater than 6. It is outside the region.
y-m-45-09.s.s2.fail.c4: The value of f=2x+2y is not 8.
y-m-45-09.s.s2.explain: If f=8 then x+y=4, and within region D this line is the segment from (4, 0) to (2, 2). Every point on this segment, such as (4, 0), (3, 1), (2.5, 1.5), (2, 2), gives the maximum 8.
y-m-45-09.s.s3.prompt: Write why the points that give the maximum are not one vertex but all the points on a segment. Also guess what happens if you change f to x+3y.
y-m-45-09.s.s3.hint.0: Write the line formed by the points where f is 8 and one side of the region in the same form, and compare them.
y-m-45-09.s.s3.hint.1: For x+3y, find the values at the four vertices and count how many points give the maximum.
y-m-45-09.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The points with the same value of f=2x+2y are ... so ...
y-m-45-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write what line the points with a constant value of f form?
y-m-45-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain the relation (overlapping, parallel) between that line and the side of the region?
y-m-45-09.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you check that for x+3y, 9 occurs only at (0, 3), so there is only one point that gives the maximum?
y-m-45-09.s.s3.model.0: 2x+2y=8 is the same line as x+y=4, so it overlaps one side of the region. At every point on that side the value is 8, the same, so the maximum is not decided as one point. If changed to x+3y, 9 occurs only at (0, 3), so there is one point.

y-m-45-10.title: Does the figure the points make change depending on the value of k?
y-m-45-10.topic: The locus of points where the sum of the squares of the distances to two fixed points is constant
y-m-45-10.goal: Explore with example points the locus of points that satisfy a condition on distances from two points, and explain why the figure becomes a circle, one point, or nothing depending on the range of the constant k.
y-m-45-10.material: On a coordinate plane there are two points A(−3, 0), B(3, 0). A point P(x, y) satisfies PA²+PB²=k (k is a constant; PA² is read 'PA squared', that is, the square of the distance between P and A). Find out how the figure that P forms changes depending on the value of k.
y-m-45-10.thinking.0: Making points that satisfy the condition yourself
y-m-45-10.thinking.1: Splitting into cases that depend on the value of the constant
y-m-45-10.prereq.0: The H2 of this task is only a difficulty level for production assignment and is not a grade assignment in the curriculum. Assume the learner has already studied middle-school linear functions (slope) and the Pythagorean theorem, and equations of lines in high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-45-10.prereq.1: The square of the distance between two points
y-m-45-10.prereq.2: The equation of a circle x²+y²=r²
y-m-45-10.prereq.3: Substituting coordinates and simplifying the expression
y-m-45-10.s.s1.prompt: For k=26, find three different points P(x, y) that satisfy PA²+PB²=26. (Decimal coordinates are fine.)
y-m-45-10.s.s1.hint.0: Decide the coordinates (x, y) of P, calculate PA² and PB², and practice adding them, starting with one point.
y-m-45-10.s.s1.hint.1: Try starting with points near the origin, and move the point depending on whether the sum is greater or less than 26.
y-m-45-10.s.s1.fail.c1: The sum of the squares of the distances between P and A and between P and B is not 26.
y-m-45-10.s.s1.explain: PA²+PB²=(x+3)²+y²+(x−3)²+y²=2x²+2y²+18. If this value is 26, then x²+y²=4, so (2, 0), (0, 2), (−2, 0), (0, −2) all satisfy the condition. (0, 0) gives 18, so it does not satisfy the condition.
y-m-45-10.s.s2.prompt: Simplifying PA²+PB²=k gives x²+y²=(k−18)/2. For k=10, 18, 26, which is the right figure that P forms?
y-m-45-10.s.s2.hint.0: For each k, first find whether the value of (k−18)/2 is positive, 0, or negative.
y-m-45-10.s.s2.hint.1: Work out what (x, y) are possible when the value of x²+y² is negative or 0.
y-m-45-10.s.s2.o.a: k=10: a circle of radius 2, k=18: the one point at the origin, k=26: a circle of radius 2
y-m-45-10.s.s2.r.a: If k=10, the right side is negative, so a sum of squares cannot be negative. Check the sign.
y-m-45-10.s.s2.o.b: k=10: nothing, k=18: the one point at the origin, k=26: a circle of radius 4
y-m-45-10.s.s2.r.b: In x²+y²=4, the radius is not 4 but the square root of 4.
y-m-45-10.s.s2.o.c: k=10: nothing, k=18: the one point at the origin, k=26: a circle of radius 2
y-m-45-10.s.s2.r.c: This is a judgment that divides into cases by the sign of the right-hand value and reads them exactly.
y-m-45-10.s.s2.o.d: k=10: nothing, k=18: nothing, k=26: a circle of radius 2
y-m-45-10.s.s2.r.d: If k=18, then x²+y²=0, so there is one point where x=0 and y=0. 0 can also be a solution.
y-m-45-10.s.s2.explain: If k=10, then x²+y²=−4, so there is no solution. If k=18, then x²+y²=0, so there is only the origin. If k=26, then x²+y²=4, so it is a circle of radius 2.
y-m-45-10.s.s3.prompt: Write for what range of k the point P forms a circle, how the radius is expressed in terms of k then, and what happens outside that range.
y-m-45-10.s.s3.hint.0: In x²+y²=(k−18)/2, think about what (x, y) are possible when the right-hand value is positive, 0, and negative.
y-m-45-10.s.s3.hint.1: To express the radius in terms of k, look at what the right-hand value must be the square of.
y-m-45-10.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If k is ..., it is a circle of radius ..., and if k is ..., ...
y-m-45-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write the range of k that makes a circle exactly, with an inequality or in words?
y-m-45-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check that the radius is the square root of (k−18)/2?
y-m-45-10.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write distinguishing the different results for k=18 and k<18?
y-m-45-10.s.s3.model.0: If k is greater than 18, then x²+y²=(k−18)/2, so it is a circle of radius √((k−18)/2). If k=18 it is the one point at the origin, and if it is less than 18 there is no such point.
y-m-45-10.s.s3.model.1: Only when k>18 is it a circle, and the radius is the square root of (k−18)/2. If k is 18 there is only one point, and if k<18 there is none.
